problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: An odd common divisor cannot disappear in the reverse process, giving the obstruction to a single final pile. Explicit binary merging and inductive reachability strategies attain the bound. Forum alternatives use modular doubling periodicity for odd totals, or a binary three-to-two reduction followed by increasing 2-adic valuation for power-of-two totals.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The largest two prime divisors of the factorial must occur in sums that are too small to be arbitrary multiples of those primes. This forces three neighboring primes into a short progression, whose residues modulo three leave only a small finite check.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Coprimality and a uniform size bound confine the recurrence to a finite set. Inverse-power residues modulo d recur by multiplicative periodicity, forcing a return to one and a chain through the target power. Another proof establishes pure periodicity from unique predecessors on the finite orbit and recovers that chain by running backwards.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2022/IMO2022SL.pdf | PDF pp. 64–65 (printed pp. 62–63), Solutions 1–3 read; tags and explanation use the complete residue and inverse-permutation arguments of Solutions 1–2 | 2026-10-16 light forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3107336p28104282; MarkBcc168 #1 statement matched. Read #2 (2023-07-08), VicKmath7 #3 (2023-07-09; edited 2024-06-10), yofro #4, vsamc #5 (2023-07-10), and #6–#9. Added orders/modular periodicity for the central Euler/inverse-power argument in #3/#5; it provides genuine support beyond the existing sequence/size/congruence/process tags. The answer is ceil(log_a d), with d<a^n<ad because gcd(a,d)=1 excludes d being a positive power of a. Bound: start each addition block below d and divide within a-1 additions, so every term is <ad. Sound return-to-one proofs are supplied by #5’s recurring inverse-power residues and #2/#7/#9’s unique-predecessor argument, after the following explicit corrections. In #2 the block contains a multiple of a, not necessarily d. In #3, choose a term immediately after a positive number of divisions whose residue returns to 1; the literal earliest k>1 with x_k=1 mod d can still lie in the initial addition block and need not be a division step. #4’s complete residue system assertion is false: inverse powers visit only the cyclic subgroup generated by a modulo d, which suffices to return to 1. #5’s isolated +a must be +d; #7’s predecessor k+d must be k-d. Reversibility is asserted on the actual bounded orbit, not as a permutation of every integer below ad; gcd(x_k,d)=1 excludes the boundary x_k=d, and the predecessor is ax_k below d or x_k-d above d. Backward powers up to the first a^n>d therefore occur. #6 reports the power a^k where the requested answer is its exponent; #9’s terminal 2^k should read a^k. All original tags and official solutions retained. Complete live statement matched; retrieved 2026-10-16T19:35:37.360Z. Prior tags and evidence preserved.

problems.explanation: AM–GM first puts the bases below a fixed fraction of the factorial index. Parity and prime-factor cases then permit LTE, whose valuation identity conflicts with Legendre's formula and the available multiples of an odd prime.

For sufficiently large n, Stirling gives a,b,c<0.4n. Odd n forces all bases even modulo 4, contradicting v_2(n!)<n-1. For even n, if an odd prime p divides b+c, then p<n and the equation forces p dividing a. It cannot divide b or c too, since v_p(n!)<n-1. LTE and the larger valuation of a^(n-1) give v_p(n!)=v_p(b+c)+v_p(n-1). These are distinct factors of n!, with b+c<n-1. Since p<=a<0.4n, there are at least two multiples of p; equality of valuations leaves only the two indicated multiples. They would be p and 2p, forcing n-1=2p, impossible for even n. Thus all pair sums are powers of two. They force equal parity of the bases, and the all-odd case is impossible. Legendre excludes all bases divisible by four. Consequently some pair sum is at most four; positivity and evenness force two bases to equal two. The third is c=2^t-2<n, and c divides n!, hence c divides 2^n. Together with c+2 a power of two, this forces c=2; then n!=3*2^(n-1) contradicts divisibility by 5 for large n. Fixed n>1 admits finitely many bases, and n=1 has no solutions. problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: The iterated equation links adjacent integer orbits, making finite versus infinite orbits the decisive split. Finite orbits yield a short period through gcd and integer bounds, followed by a least-nonzero-value contradiction. Infinite orbits have consistent meeting-time offsets that force a translation.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2020/IMO2020SL.pdf | PDF pp. 24–25 (printed pp. 22–23), Sole solution, both orbit cases, gcd period bound and meeting-time-offset argument; only rigid solution families arise, so no monsters tag | 2026-10-17 light live forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2625860p22698062; Live Eyed #1 complete integer-domain iterated equation matched. Both derive f(-1)=0 and f^(a^2)(a)=a*f(a)=f^(a^2+1)(a-1). Adjacent orbit tails therefore meet with time offset one, so all integer orbits are finite or all are infinite. In #4 finite case, a bound on the orbit of zero forces f(a)=f(-a) for sufficiently large absolute a by integrality. Comparing the two equal orbit tails then forces f(a)=0 there. Returns of zero at times a^2-1 for all large a have gcd one, so f(0)=0. Taking a and a+b large in the original equation gives f(b)=0 for every b. #10 instead first uses the returns 2a^2 and 2(a+1)^2 to obtain f^2(0)=0; symmetry and substitutions at a and -a give f(a)=0 for all nonzero a, and return times 3 and 8 force f(0)=0. In the infinite case, the common-tail identity gives f^N(a+1)=f^(N+f(a)-a-1)(a+1) for large N. An unequal time shift repeats a value and makes that orbit finite, so f(a)=a+1. Negative offsets are handled by taking N sufficiently large. The two families satisfy the original equation, including exponent zero at a=b=0. #2 is not used as a complete proof: its opening assertion allowing arbitrary f(0) when all other values vanish is false (f(0)=2 fails at a=b=1), and f(x)>x alone does not imply injectivity. #6 has a valid finite-orbit argument, but its infinite branch applies an identity established only for positive a to a=f^k(0) without showing that value is positive. The complete #4/#10 proofs supply the classification. No tags or explanation changed; existing official extremal and arithmetic support retained. problems.subject: A
problems.explanation: A dyadic partition bounds each class by a telescoping square-root sum, and Cauchy combines the class sizes. The second proof splits the sequence inductively and uses a telescoping product plus a logarithmic estimate to control the remaining block.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2020/IMO2020SL.pdf | PDF pp. 26–27 (printed pp. 24–25), Solutions 1–2 and the intervening comments read; the optional adjacent-exchange normalization is not used for additional tags | 2026-10-17 light live forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2625876p22698187; Live IndoMathXdZ #1 complete n,k and [1,2^k] statement matched. For a block in [1,2], the reciprocal square-root sum is at most 2*sqrt(m), while the squared-numerator sum telescopes to at most 4*sqrt(m). Cauchy gives a bound 2*sqrt(2m), which is stronger than 4*sqrt(m). Rescaling and grouping indices into k disjoint dyadic classes, preserving their original order, only decreases the denominators when outside terms are discarded. Cauchy on class sizes gives the desired 4*sqrt(k*n); repeated values are counted by their distinct indices, not as a set without multiplicity. #7 supplies the complete induction alternative: put x_j=a_j/sqrt(S_j), with S_j the partial square sum. Products of 1-x_j^2 telescope to a ratio of two partial sums, at least 1/(4^k+1) for the second half-block. Hence that half has square sum at most log(4^k+1)<=2k, and Cauchy controls its ordinary sum. Strong induction separately handles even and odd n; n<=16k supplies the base range and guarantees the stated odd-case size condition. Its product lemma is used only for 0<=u_j<1, where multiplying e^(-u_j)>=1-u_j is valid; its claim for arbitrary real u_j is too broad and is not used. The logarithmic bound follows, for example, from e^2>5 and 5^k>=4^k+1 for integer k>=1. These proofs corroborate every existing method label. The original equation gives B+y=A*f(y)+1. If A=0 this is impossible for all y, so A>0 and f is affine. problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The inequalities force the permutation to decompose into fixed singletons and swapped adjacent pairs. This gives both a Fibonacci deletion recurrence and a bijection with monomer–domino tilings of a strip.

Thus the suffix contains exactly i through n, and i must occur at position n. For i<=n-2, the next-to-last inequality forces a_(n-1)<=i, impossible since i has already been used. Hence n is last, or n and n-1 occupy the last two positions in swapped order. Deleting that singleton or adjacent pair gives the recurrence T_n=T_(n-1)+T_(n-2), with T_1=1,T_2=2, so T_n=F_(n+1). #6 gives a sound alternate contradiction via (n-1)*a_(n-1)=n*i and gcd(n-1,n)=1. In its first induction case a_i<=i-3 must read a_(i-1)<=i-3; the subsequent upper-bound contradiction invokes that proved lower bound. These bounds force only fixed singletons and disjoint adjacent swaps, yielding the existing strip-tiling interpretation. #4 agrees with that exclusion, but its case-2 display must be n*(n-1)<=n*a_n, its tail value a_n=n-1, and its recurrence T_n=T_(n-1)+T_(n-2); #5 abbreviates that exclusion, supplied explicitly by #2/#6. #3 is not used: its Bertrand step incorrectly claims that the chosen prime divides only one number in an interval of k+1 consecutive integers. problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: A stronger polygon statement permits induction while preserving enough vertices of each color. Counting blocks finds a suitable consecutive quadruple, whose removal leaves a smaller convex polygon and keeps the constructed quadrilaterals disjoint. A forum alternative discards one vertex and preserves opposite color-count parity while repeatedly deleting a majority-color quadrilateral.

Removing four consecutive vertices of the remaining strictly convex polygon separates that quadrilateral from the convex hull of all later vertices, ensuring disjointness. Both counts decrease by odd numbers, so their opposite parity is preserved and equality cannot occur. The first nine steps lead to (31,32); then the majority alternates with difference one until (2,1), after exactly 24 removals. Thus both colors remain available at every required step. #12 independently discards three arbitrary vertices; its termination assertion is justified as follows. Initially the minority is at least 38 and the odd count difference at most 21; at most ten steps reduce the difference to 1 while both counts remain positive. Thereafter the difference stays 1; losing the last minority vertex can only occur at counts (2,1), since the total remains 1 modulo 4, leaving one vertex. problems.explanation: Each company's directed links split the checkpoints into disjoint increasing chains. Assigning a checkpoint its two chain labels gives a pigeonhole bound, while block chains versus residue-class chains supply the matching obstruction.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Selected odd-index Fibonacci differences form a graph whose cycles are excluded by a telescoping growth identity. The forest edge bound forces the set size, and even-index Fibonacci values give an explicit attaining construction. A forum alternative recursively splits the graph after deleting its two largest labels, bounding all distinct Fibonacci differences.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2020/IMO2020SL.pdf | PDF pp. 36 (printed pp. 34), Sole solution, acyclic difference graph and attaining set; the isolated F5 in the displayed even-index set is a typo for F6, as the following verification makes clear | 2026-10-17 light live forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2625914p22698447; Live MathLuis #1 full Fibonacci-difference statement matched (2021-07-20, edited 2022-04-19). A cycle largest label F_(2j+1) would be at most the sum of its other, distinct smaller odd labels, which is at most F_(2j)<F_(2j+1). The graph is a forest, not necessarily the tree claimed in #3; its ceil(n/2) edges force at least ceil(n/2)+1 vertices. The attaining set is {F0,F2,...,F_(2*ceil(n/2))}: each even value is its difference from zero, and F_(2j-1)=F_(2j)-F_(2j-2). The symbol d in #2 is ceil(n/2). #5 gives a sound independent stronger bound: a set of m>=2 integers has at most 2m-3 distinct positive Fibonacci differences. Retain one edge per distinct difference; delete the largest label F_t and the F_(t-1) edge if present. No remaining path can join the largest-edge endpoints, since its distinct labels sum to at most F2+...+F_(t-2)=F_t minus 2. Split the disconnected graph into two nonempty vertex sets. For m>=3 one part has size at least two, so induction bounds their edges by 2m1-3 and 2m2-2, with at most two deleted edges restored; base m=1 has zero and m=2 at most one edge. Thus n-1<=2m-3 gives the same sharp answer. problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: A hypothetical occurrence of every target proportion gives distinct integer hitting times. Monotonic counts of both colors constrain their relative sizes, and choosing maximal earlier times forces one past the allowed range.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2020/IMO2020SL.pdf | PDF pp. 38–39 (printed pp. 36–37), Sole solution, hitting-time inequalities and both extremal cases; small-prime sharpness examples read separately | 2026-10-17 light live forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2625882p22698214; Live vvluo #1 full two-color proportion statement matched (2021-07-20, edited same day). Read nukelauncher #2 (2021-07-20, solution expanded) and L567 #12 (2023-05-27). Both give sound extremal hitting-time arguments. Since p is prime, every occurrence of a/p is at a distinct positive multiple of p. Scale these times as k_i, so all k_i<(p^2-1)/4. If k_i<k_j, monotone red and blue counts give j*k_j>=i*k_i and (p-j)*k_j>=(p-i)*k_i. Swap colors to put k_1<k_(p-1). With h=(p-1)/2, if all k_1,...,k_h precede k_(p-1), their maximal time is at least h and forces k_(p-1)>=h*(p-h)=(p^2-1)/4. Otherwise let ell>=1 be maximal with k_1,...,k_ell before k_(p-1). Then ell<h, some earlier k_i>=ell, and p-i>=(p+1)/2. Consequently k_(p-1)>=ell*(p+1)/2, while k_(ell+1)>k_(p-1) forces k_(ell+1)>=(p-1)*k_(p-1)/(ell+1)>=(p^2-1)/4. This also handles p=3 via the first case. In #12 the complement replaces k_i by k_(p-i), not p-k_i, and its final explanatory phrase p-1 must read p-i. These are notation errors; the displayed bound and complete argument are valid with those repairs. #2 independently partitions the lower-half target indices according to whether their first hitting time precedes that for p-1. If all precede, the maximal earlier time gives the same threshold. Otherwise its least later target m>=2 has at least m-1 lower targets before p-1, yielding f(m)>=p*(p+1)*(p-1)*(m-1)/(2*m)>=N+1. The positivity and distinct-time hypotheses used in this bound are satisfied. No tags or explanation changed; these methods corroborate the existing extremal/global and integer-rigidity labels. Other cached replies not certified complete proofs. Complete assessed mathematics and displayed metadata cached. Retrieved 2026-10-17T16:46:14.969Z. Every prior tag and source caveat preserved.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Pairing complementary weights converts the allocation into splitting a 4-regular multigraph into two equal-degree edge colors, achieved along Euler circuits. The alternative chooses auxiliary monochromatic matchings with a minimum number of cycles, then switches edges to force the needed cycle lengths. A forum alternative solves a consistent system over the two-element field to construct monochromatic pairings and alternating cycles.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2020/IMO2020SL.pdf | PDF pp. 40–41 (printed pp. 38–39), Solutions 1–2, Euler-circuit coloring and minimum-component matching-switch construction | 2026-10-17 light live forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2278652p17821656; Live Aryan-23 #1 full pebble statement matched (2020-09-22, edited by djmathman 2020-10-06); also main IMO 2020 P3. Each color vertex has degree four, counting a loop twice. Each component with v vertices therefore has 2v edges, so alternating its Euler circuit also alternates across the final/first edge. Every color receives degree two in each edge class, hence two pebbles per pile; n complementary pairs give weight n*(4n+1). The required parity is per component, not merely the even global edge count. #16 supplies a sound materially different algebraic construction. Over F2 impose x_i+x_(4n+1-i)=1 for each complementary pair and sum(x_i in a color quadruple)=0. A zero combination of coefficient rows uses k pair equations and m color equations. Because each family partitions the variables, cancellation requires exactly the same variable support and 2k=4m, so k is even and the combined right side is zero. Thus no inconsistent 0=1 relation exists, proving solvability; merely having more variables than equations would not suffice. Within each quadruple, pair equal x labels, possible since its four labels have even sum. The union of these monochromatic pairs with the complementary pairs is a disjoint union of alternating cycles: complementary edges flip x and monochromatic edges preserve x, so each cycle has an even number of complementary edges and length divisible by four. Select alternate complementary edges around each cycle; every monochromatic pair is split between piles. This proves both requirements for arbitrary colors, beyond the initial even-sum special case in #16. problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Dominance maps between row and column sets are iterated until their images stabilize, producing a smaller saddle pair unless the cardinalities agree. A second inductive argument forces bijections, and summing a permuted chain of inequalities makes every entrywise inequality an equality.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2020/IMO2020SL.pdf | PDF pp. 42–45 (printed pp. 40–43), Solutions 1–2 and Comment 1, stabilized image maps, minimality lemma, induction and equality under bijections | 2026-10-17 light live forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2625884p22698238; Live popcorn1 #1 complete saddle-pair statement matched (2021-07-20, edited same day). Fix row dominance maps R1 to R2 to R1 with composite f, and column dominance maps C1 to C2 to C1 with composite g. The selected second-stage image depends only on the intermediate row, so |f(R1)|<=|R2|<|R1|. Their four dominance inequalities give a(r,g(c))<=a(f(r),c) for every r in R1,c in C1. The iterated images f^j(R1),g^j(C1) are nested finite nonempty sets and stabilize to E,D; f and g restrict to permutations there. Choose a common multiple M of their permutation orders beyond stabilization. For c in D, iterating a(r,c)<=a(f(r),g^(-1)(c)) yields a(r,c)<=a(f^M(r),c); combined with the original saddle row condition, E dominates all rows on D. For r in E, iterating the forward inequality yields a(r,g^M(c))<=a(r,c); combined with the original column condition, D dominates all columns on E. Thus (E,D) is a saddle subpair with E a proper subset of R1, contradicting minimality. Finite permutation orders, rather than just finitely many image sets, justify the common exponent. The final sentence of #4 applies to pairs of unequal row cardinality, not arbitrary saddle pairs. #5 is not certified: its first saddle-subpair claim asserts that f^X(t) lies in A subset R, but multiplying an entrance time by column-cycle periods does not justify retaining the required row-side membership under its alternating maps. No extra tag or proof is inferred from that unresolved step. #2/#3 only link to a paper, not substantive forum proofs. problems.explanation: It suffices to add a set U, disjoint from S, with Σ(U) = arctan(b/a) when Σ(S) = arctan(a/b). Taking l = ⌊a/b⌋+1 and peeling off arctan(1/l) leaves a fraction with strictly smaller numerator, so induction builds U; repeated values or collisions with S are removed by arctan(1/t) = arctan(1/(t+1)) + arctan(1/(t²+t+1)), applied until all values are new.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Composing with f reduces the task to writing the identity as u + v with u, v bijections. Build u and v as odd functions step by step: each new odd argument of u is sent to minus the smallest positive integer not yet attained, each new even argument of v likewise, and the partner function takes the complementary value; this back-and-forth choice hits every integer and stays injective.

problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Split N = N1·N2 with N1 dividing a power of a and N2 coprime to a. Choose C with C·N1 | a^C and a large prime p ≡ 1 (mod φ(N2)). For n = Cp, Fermat gives ⌊a^n/n⌋ = (a^(Cp) − a^C)/(Cp) = (a^C/C)·(a^(C(p−1)) − 1)/p, whose first factor is divisible by N1 and second by N2.

problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: Triangulate the point set. If the convex hull has k ≤ 4n vertices, there are 2n²+4n−k ≥ 2n² triangles inside a square of area n², so one has area at most 1/2. If k > 4n, the hull perimeter is at most 4n, so two consecutive sides have total length at most 2, and by AM–GM the triangle they span has area at most 1/2.
